lawyer:
Dr Kamal Hossain with Sara Hossain with Ramzan Ali Sikder, Advocates -----For the Petitioner.
 Fazia Haque, Advocate ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Abul Khair Condensed Milk and Beverage Ltd ----- Petitioner 
Vs.
Commissioner of Customs and ors ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: In the above Rule Nisi legality of three CRF certificates issued on 20-10-05 in respect of the imported sugar was challenged and a direction was sought for assessment of said goods on the basis of invoice value as normal/transaction value.

2. The petitioner is stated to be a company incorporated in Bangladesh under the Companies Act. It imported 22,700 metric tons of sugar from Brazil by opening three letters of credit on 24-8-05, 27-8-05 and 28-8-05 at the rate of US$ 260 permetricton, Before shipment the goods were inspected by an approved PSI agency and arrived with three CRF certificates issued by said PSI agency. After arrival of the goods at Chittagong Port four bills of entry were submitted on 2-11-05 for clearance of the goods for home consumption. Upon receipt of the bills of entry the customs authority assessed the goods to duty on the basis of the value certified in the CRF certificates at the rate of US$ 262 per metric ton and printed computerised generated bills of entry, Annexure-'E' series to the writ petition.

3. During the vacation, the petitioner challenged such CRF certificates before a Single Bench of this Division and on 9-11-05 obtained an order of  release of the goods on payment of duty and other charges in cash on the basis of invoice value and upon further receipt of 25 percent of the CRF value in cash and rest 75 percent upon receipt of continuing bank guarantee(s).

4. On behalf of the respondent No. 1, the Commissioner of Customs on 15-11-05 made an application for vacating aforesaid interim order of release. In the application, it is denied that the goods were assessed to duty on receipt of the bills of entry on the basis of CRF certified value. It was stated that no assessment of duty was at all made. It was further stated that said CRF agency in collusion with the petitioner certified a price at much lower than the prevalent price. Because of the dishonest valuation, the customs authority suffered loss of Taka 6,42,62,862.42 in revenue.

5. Against the application the petitioner on 20-11-95 filed an affidavit-in-opposition denying what was claimed therein and reiterated what were stated in the writ petition. On 15-11-07 the application was ordered for hearing on 17-11-05 and the above Rule was issued as aforesaid. Ultimately, the application was ordered to be kept with the file by order dated 27-11-05.

6. Then, said respondent No.1 on 7-5-07 submitted an affidavit-in-opposition to the writ petition. In the affidavit, it was stated that pursuant to the order of release of this Division, the goods were released on the basis of a provisional assessment. It was again reiterated that before the goods could be assessed to duty the petitioner moved this Division and first, obtained the release order and then, the Rule.

7. It also annexed a demand notice dated 16-11-05 for aforesaid Taka 6,42,62,862.42 under section 32 of the Customs Act, 1969 and the goods were valued at the rate of US$ 319.74 per metric ton at the prevalent rate of international price.

8. On 30-4-07 the petitioner filed a supplementary affidavit annexing the correspondences between the petitioner and the supplier. In said affidavit, it was stated that the supplier informed the petitioner that the PSI agency did never ask the supplier for any information/data for the present market price nor did it obtain any information/date from the supplier on the price of the goods on any specific form whatsoever.

Said respondent on 13-5-07 submitted a supplementary affidavit-in-opposition seeking some corrections in their affidavit-in-opposition dated 7-5-07.

9. The petitioner on 17-5-07 submitted an affidavit-in-reply. In the affidavit, it is stated mainly that the respondent No. 1 provided no objective basis for the allegations that the invoice value did not reflect the current market price of sugar as prevailing on the date of issuance of invoice i.e. 3rd and 4th October 2005, nor had he taken any necessary steps to determine the current market price through any of the established procedures for doing so.

10. Respondent No. 1 then on 2-8-07 filed further supplementary affidavit-in-opposition in said affidavit, he denied the case of the petitioner that on receipt of the bills of entry the goods were assessed to duty on the basis of the value certified in the CRF certificates and computerised bills of entry were printed out. It was further stated that annexed bills of entry did not contain any order of assessment.

11. The procedure the customs authority has been following what is called "Journey of Computerised Bill of Entry under ASYCUDA "System" meaning Automated System of Customs Data, Plus Plus indicating modifications done twice for betterment of the software of the said computer system was elaborately described as hereunder:

i.To release the consignment of imported goods the importer himself or his C&F agent fills up the Biil of Entry Form and fixes all necessary documents concerning the import along with the said Form, a specimen of which is Annexure-X. The importer or his agent put signatures on two copies of Lodgment Slip, Annexure-X-1. Then, the importer or Agent submits the Bill of Entry to the Import General Manifest (IGM) Section under section 79 of the Customs Act for noting;

ii. Said IGM section examines the particulars of filled up Bill of Entry Form and Bill of Lading, Import Manifest, etc and if found correct, makes noting of the Bill of Entry and sends the same (which is also known as Data Sheet) to the pre-Entry Check Section;

iii. The Pre-Entry Check section puts all the documents with the Bill of Entry in a Plastic Folder and ascertains that all the documents have been attached and then, gives a Folder Number on the lodgement slip and supplies a copy of the Lodgment. Slip to the importer or his Agent. Then this pre-Entry Check section sends the Folder and other copies of Lodgment Slip to the Head Assistant of the Computer Hall. Then the Head Assistant of the Computer Hall distributes the Folders to the Data Entry Operators. The concerned Data Entry Operator enters the particualrs or information given in the filled up Bill of Entry in the computer (which is also known as Making Entry in the ASYCUDA++ programme). According to the programme in the computer, the computer gives a serial number which is known as Registration Number or BE number (Bill of Entry Number). The operator takes out 3 copies of print of the Bill of Entry with the said number. In this way, at the time of registration of the Bill of Entry the name of the Appraiser or officer of Customs who will assess the duty also gets computerised and kept in the computer.

iv. Thereafter, concerned computer operator writes down the name of the appraiser upon the Lodgment Slip and number of Bill of Entry and sends the folder to the lodgment counter, through the Head Assistant of the Computer Hall, From the lodgment counter, the printed Bill of Entry or Data Sheet reaches to the Appraiser through Transit Section. The Bill of Entry at this stage looks like as Annexure-X-2 From the beginning up to this stage, the process is known as Bill of Entry Noting and registration process under section 79 of the Customs Act;

v. The Appraiser then examines the documents and makes Assessment of customs duty under section 80 of Customs Act and sends the papers to the Principal Appraiser for confirmation of assessment and for issue of Assessment Notice. But when there is any necessity for compliance with some regulation say Import Policy such as radiation test of food items, for example Apple, then without making any assessment the Appraiser sends the goods for Readiation Test;

vi. When the Bill of Entry comes to the Principal Appraiser, he examines the papers and follows the principles for assessment in respect of the imported goods and if he finds them correct, confirms the assessment and from his computer takes out 3 copies of prints of the Assessment Notice. At the time of printing the Assessment Notice, an Assessment Number is automatically put on the Bill of Entry according to the computer programme. After assessment and customs duty the concerned Appraiser and Principal Appraiser put their signatures with respective seals on the Assessment Notice. After the completion of all these, it is called that Assessment has been done. The Assessment Notice, looks as Annexure-X-4;

vii. Thereafter, the signed Bill of Entry along with Assessment Notice and all the documents in the Plastic Folder are presented to the Section Assistant who sees whether all the documents are there. From the documents, he finds out the original Bill of Lading, letter of credit, etc and gives them to the C&F Agent. There after Emboss Seals are given on the Bill of Entry and Assessment Notice. After putting seals, 3rd copy of the Bill of Entry is kept in the concerned section of asessment, the other two copies are given to the C&F Agent. And three copies of Assessment Notice are sent to the Delivery Counter. From the Delivery Counter, the Assessment Notice along with other papers are sent to the concerned Sonali Bank. The Bank Authority gives Emboss Seal on the Assessment Notice and realises payment of customs duty. After realisation of the duty the said Bank keeps 3rd copy of the Asessment Notice and sends 2 other copies to the Treasury Speed Branch (or Delivery Branch.);

viii. That computer operators of the Treasury Speed Branch examine as to whether there are seals and signatures of the Delivery Counter, Appraiser and Principal Appraiser and duty is realised and after such scrutiny he prints the Release Order. When the Release Order is printed according to the computer programme a number is automatically put in the Release Order, which is the Release Order Number (or R N) Annexure-X-5. The operator puts his signature on the printed Release Order and then sends it to the Head Assistant of the Section; and

ix. The Head Assistant puts his signature upon the Release Order and Release order Number is perforated by Punch Machine and given to the other Assistant of the section (Treasury Speed Section or Delivery Section. The Assistant keeps the 2nd copy of the Assessment Notice in the Speed Section and hands over the original copy of Assessment Notice to the C and F agent. He also gives the 1st and 2nd copy of the Release Order to the C&F Agent. Then, the C&F Agent takes steps for taking delivery of imported goods.

12. It is further stated that the remedy against CRF certificate in a particular case was available under Paragraph 9 of the Pre-shipment Inspection Order, 1999 and “বিরোধ নিষ্পত্তি কমিটি” formed under rule 23 of Pre-shipment Inspection Rules 2002 vide office order dated 12-9-05, Annexure-5 to the affidavit. But the remedy was not available to the petitioner since the letters of credit were opened by the petitioner before September 01, 2005, Said order was applicable only in cases where letter of credit was opened after September 1, 2005.

13. The petitioner on 13-9-07 filed another supplementary affidavit. In said affidavit, it was stated that the “বিরোধ নিষ্পত্তি” which the respondent referred to in the affidavit dated 29-8-07 was established in September, 2005 did not function for some time and, as such the petitioner could not avail of any remedy before such committee. It further reiterated that the review committee was established on 5-7-06 by an order of the National Board of Revenue long after the impugned order was passed. The petitioner therefore could not even seek remedy before the review committee as was stated to be formed on 20-5-01. Pursuant to rule 36 of aforesaid PSI Rules, 2002 it was stated that such rule related to pending matters or proceedings after coming into force of the PSI Rules, 2002 after repeal of the PSI Order, 1999 and did not cover the present case.

14. By filing further explanation, on white sheets of paper on behalf of respondent No. 1, it is stated that in the case the petitioner opened letter of credit on 24-8-05 mentioning the name of respondent No. 4 as PSI agency, which was appointed under the PSI Order, 1999 and whose service was extended up to 31-8-05 by memorandum dated 30-6-05. Then, new PSI agencies were appointed under the PSI Rules, 2002 with effect from 1st September 2005 vide the notification being SRO No. 153 dated 23-8-05, Annexure-F2 to the writ petition. The petitioner could file complaint, if any, in respect of the PSI certificates before the review committee appointed under said Rules.

15. Dr Kamal Hossain, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, challenged the certificates issued by the respondent No. 4, PSI agency mainly on the grounds that those were issued at inflated value without following the mandatory provisions of the PSI Rules, 2002.

16. He submitted that in view of the disclosures of the supplier, Annexure-K series that the PSI Agent did not ask the supplier for any information data of the present market price nor did it obtain any data or information on the price of the imported goods, the customs authority most illegally and arbitrarily assessed he goods to duty upon such PS certified value.

17. He also tried to impress upon us that in view of print out of computerised bills of entry with all necessary information/data entered therein though without the date, signature and seal of the appropriate customs authority the assertion of the customs authority that the goods was not assessed to duty had got no basis.

18. Lastly, he submitted that in view of release of the imported goods pursuant to the interim order of this Division dated 11-9-05 upon receipt of the duty and other charges both in cash and upon bank guarantee(s), the customs authority would now assess the goods finally to duty in accordance with law by ignoring the CRF certificates.

19. In support, he cited Showkat Ali vs Commissioner of Customs 6 BLC 357 and Alhaj Nazir Ahmed vs National Board of Revenue 2001 BLD 59.

20. Mr Fazlul Haque, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of said respondent No. 1, on the other hand, submitted that the goods were not assessed to duty and before any assessment could be made the petitioner obtained the interim release order and got the goods cleared.

21. He submitted that copies of computerised generated bills of entry were never supplied by the customs authority to the petitioner and those copies were no proof of the fact that the goods were assessed to duty on the basis of CRF certified value, which contained no date, signature and/or seal of the appropriate authority and not even an order of assessment and assessment notice.

22. He submitted that the petitioner obtained the CRF certificates by way of collusion with the PSI agency at much lower price than the international price of the imported goods and also release of the goods pursuant to the interim order of this Division, which caused revenue loss of Taka 6,42,62,862.42 if the goods could be assessed to, duty at the rate of US$ 319.74 per metric ton at the relevant time and the customs authority had to issue a demand notice dated 16-11-05.

23. He submitted that the customs authority had never accepted and assessed the duty at the value certified by the PSI agency and the Rule issued before assessment of the goods to duty must be held to be premature and would be liable to be discharged on this count only.

24. In the aforesaid pleadings and on the submissions of the learned Advocate number of issues was raised. But, in view of the order that we may have to pass ultimately in disposing of the Rule, we are afraid we could deal and dispose of them exhaustively in this writ petition.

25. First, both parties seriously differed on the question of assessment of the goods, namely, sugar of Brazilian origin to duty. It is the case of the petitioner, importer that it challenged the CRF certificates when the customs authority assessed the goods to duty on the inflated value certified therein. In support, computer generated bills of entry were annexed. Its main grievance against the CRF certificates is that they were issued violating the mandatory provisions of rule 13 of the PSI Rules, 2002.

26. On the other hand, it is the definite case of respondent No.1, the Commissioner of Customs, that before the imported goods could be assessed to duty the petitioner moved. this Division on the allegations that the goods was assessed to duty on the basis of CRF certified value and upon such misrepresentation obtained the Rule and release of the goods; that the computerised generated print out is no proof of assessment and the petitioner was not supposed to receive such print out before assessment; that such print out is lacking signature, seal and date of respective customs officers and more particularly, order of assessment cannot be read as assessment and that after assessment in all cases, an assessment order and assessment notice are issued and before issue of such order and notice there is no scope for reading any paper that may be obtained from the office of respondent No.1 as assessment.

27. What is assessment has not been defined in the Customs Act, 1969. Section 79 requires only for the owner of the imported goods to make entry of such goods for home consumption or any other purpose by delivering to an appropriate officer the bill of entry in such form and containing such particulars as the National Board of Revenue may direct. After receipt of such bill of entry, under section 80 the goods shall be assessed to duty, if any and the owner of such goods may then proceed to clear the same for home consumption or warehousing subject to other provisions of the Act. Section 79A was though inserted long back on 1st July 1999 but the customs authority is not yet prepared to take step for acceptance of electronically transmitted bills of entry and/or documents. Section 79B to 790 was inserted by Act No. 15 of 2000. Section 79B provides for access as a user to the computer system by being registered with the Commissioner of Customs, None of the benefits thought to be user friendly could be availed of for the delay in the introduction of the system.

28. The procedure for assessment the customs authority has been following as was stated hereinabove in detail is no doubt lengthy and elaborate and nay seem to be complicated. But after the time for completion of assessment is clamped and prescribed, the customs authority is obliged to complete their job with all the limitations in the prescribed time frame. During such time prescribed for assessment, no importer should or could have any grievance. Rather, he should cooperate with the customs authority to obviate all problems in the clearance of the imported goods.

<u>29. Situation is not different in any way in the neighboring countries, which have got rich experience in working under the same for similar law. Mrs Sara Hossain, learned Advocate, studied on the process of assessment in neighboring  jurisdictions but she also could not find any legal rules for assessment. Assessment is really a matter of national revenue and the National Board of Revenue runs the show by issuing notifications etc time to time on the basis of broader guidelines promulgated in the Finance Act of a year.</u>

<u>30 . There should not be any doubt in the fact that every assessment either of income tax or VAT or excise presupposes existence of an order of assessment. It is equally true in the case of assessment of duty under the Customs Act. When no assessment assessing duty on the imported goods could be shown, only conclusion could be arrived at law is that there was no assessment. Any grievance raised or brought against such inchoate assessment must be held to be based on supposition of an assessment and does not deserve any consideration. Consequently, the rights and obligations arising out of assessment could only be agitated and decided only in accordance with law. This Division is generally not empowered to intervene in the process of assessment. In all the cases cited and relied upon by Dr Kamal this Division intervened only after assessment of duty.</u>

31. In the case at hand, the papers annexed and relied upon by the petitioner do not constitute an assessment of duty on the imported goods. In the circumstances, we have got no hesitation to say that the above Rule was obtained before any assessment of the goods to duty could be made and was issued prematurely.

32. Then, the parties differed seriously on the CRF certificates. It is the case of the petitioner that said certificates were issued at an inflated rate much higher than the international price and in violation of some mandatory provisions of the PSI Rules, 2002. On the other hand, the customs authority found the value certified by PSI agency much lower than the international price at the relevant time of submission of bills of entry.

33. We are amazed and, amused at the lengthy and strenuous arguments of the learned Advocates. Few facts may help understand the basis of the bone of contention of the parties. The petitioner imported 22,500 metric ton of sugar of Brazilian origin at the rate of US$ 260 per metric ton. The PSI agency certified the value of sugar at US$ 262 in its certificates. The customs authority found the value certified in the said certificates much lower than the international price. In his demand notice, issued on behalf of respondent No. 1 sugar was valued at the rate of US$ 319.74 per metric ton as the then market price. After hearing such learned submissions one thing becomes clear that none of the parties was happy at the service of the PSI agency.

34. Sections 25A was inserted in the Customs Act by Act No. 11 of 1994 with effect from July 1, 1994 and section 25B and 25C were inserted by Act No. 15 of 2000 with effect from 15-2-2000. Section 25A was time to time substituted to take the present shape, which is effective since July 1, 1999.

35. Section 25A empowers the Government to appoint pre-shipment agencies and audit agencies for certification and audit mainly on the inspection and certification of imported goods. By notification in official gazette, the government is also empowered to declare that the quality, quantity, price, description and customs classification of any goods verified and certified in the prescribed manner by a pre-shipment inspection agency shall be accepted as the basis for assessment. Section 25B requires all imported goods to be inspected by an approved preshipment agency subject to exemption granted by the Government by notification in the official gazette. And 25C provides for imposition and collection of pre-shipment inspection service charge as a customs duty at a rate not exceeding one percent ad-valorem.

36. In order to carry out the purpose of the above provisions of pre-inspection of imported goods and certification by approved pre-shipment agency, the notification being SRO No. 316 dated 19-10-99 was published, naming it as the Pre-Shipment Inspection Order, 1999. In such Order, everything right from appointment and service of pre-shipment agencies and resolution of disputes that may arise out of such service and certification of goods and time limit for completion of assessment and release of imported goods at the earliest were prescribed. Then, by notification being SRO No. 255 dated 19-9-2000 as the Pre-shipment Inspection Rules, 2002 was published and the previous Order was repealed. In the present Rules, procedure for certification of the imported goods, forum for resolution of disputes that may arise from the certification and time limit for completion of assessment, etc in all detail were prescribed.

37. In the Order, 1999 a review committee was conceived for resolution of all 'disputes regarding the certification by the PSI agency. Section 193C of the Customs Act, 1969 was accordingly updated providing for review of any matter related to the Clean Report of Findings (CRF) issued by the pre-shipment inspection agencies. Then, after introduction of the PSI Rules, 2002, a five member “বিরোধ নিষ্পত্তি কমিটি” for resolution of disputes was first thought of, which was replaced by a notification being SRO No. 154 dated 21-6-06 by previous provision of review committee. There is dispute over which was the forum available to the petitioner at the time. On behalf of the customs authority, it was sometimes asserted that the petitioner ought to go to the “বিরোধ নিষ্পত্তি কমিটি” but on the next breath, asked the petitioner to go the review committee if it has got grievance against the certification of the imported goods. On behalf of the petitioner, it is claimed that the “বিরোধ নিষ্পত্তি কমিটি” claimed to be established in September, 2005 was not working and the review committee was formed on 5-7-06 long after the impugned assessment. We must admit that we have failed to ascertain first, what was the forum available during the time of submission of bills of entry on 2-11-05 and second, if there was any, was it working. This dispute over the forum ultimately appears to be of no significance in view of rule 23(2) of the PSI Rules, 2002 that an importer could be aggrieved only after clearance of the goods and then, he may seek redress against the certification of the goods.

38. At the end of the day, in spite of the above detailed and comprehensive provisions providing the basis for assessment of duty, it appears that the system brought into operation could please neither the importer nor the customs authority. Mechanism for resolution of disputes could not satisfy the importers. May be for this reason, this Division was flooded with writs against the certification of the goods and/or delay in the process of assessment of duty. Search for the actual price, that is, "the price actually paid or payable, or the nearest ascertainable equivalent of such price" remains as the golden deer, সোনার হরিণ as before.

39. Now, the grievance against the CRF certificates on the premise of assessment appears to be of no foundation. When the goods were not at all assessed to duty, all submissions against such certificates appear to be premature. It is for the customs authority first to consider and decide on the certification of the goods as to whether the CT certificate was correct and in order with regard quality, quantity, price, description and custom classification of the imported goods and provides the basis for assessment, and could act and assess the duty thereon. This Division is not empowered to preempt the power of the customs authority in respect of such certification and decide on such CRF certificates before assessment. In all the cases cited on behalf of the petitioner, this Division considered and decided on the legality of such CRF certificates only after assessment.

40. Saying all and everything in disposing of the issues raised, we cannot leave here the goods were cleared pursuant to an interim order of this Division, which now needs to be finally assessed. When none of the parties could accept the CRF certificates, only option is now left to the customs authority that is under sub-rule (2) of rule 22 of the PSI Rules, 2002 to ascertain the value and HS Code of the goods in accordance with the Customs Valuation Rules, 2000. It is needless to say that in the process, the petitioner shall be at liberty to produce any document/paper in support of the invoice value, which the customs authority shall consider in finally assessing the goods.

41. Before we part with the case, we must express our view about the demand notice dated 16-11-05, Annexure-4 to supplementary affidavit-in-opposition dated 7-5-07, which put the petitioner into natural anxiety. It is a fact now that the goods were released on or about 16-11-05 pursuant to the interim order of this Division. On the same date the customs authority issued a demand notice asking the petitioner to pay Taka 6,42,62,862.42, which they arrived at the rate of US$ 319.74 per metric tons of sugar rejecting the CRF certificates. They claim the demand was issued under section 32 of the Customs Act.

42. Section 32 of the Customs Act comprises of 2 parts. Sub-section (1) makes it offence to make or sign or causes to be made or signed, or delivers or causes to be delivered to an officer of customs any declaration, notice, certificate or other document, or makes any statement in answer to any question, or transmits any statement, document, information or record etc and such document or statement is untrue in any material particular.

43. Sub-section (2), on the other hand, makes one liable to pay any amount by reason of any such document or statement as aforesaid or by reason of some collusion any duty or charge has not been levied or has been short-levied or has been erroneously refunded and requires a notice to be served upon such person within three years of relevant date to show cause why he should not pay the amount specified therein. The proviso to sub-section (5) of section 32 describes the expression, "relevant date."

44. In view of above provisions and in the facts of the case, issue of such demand notice has got no legal basis and must be held to be ex facie bad. Moreover, none of the provisions under the section could be invoked before assessment of duty and clearance of the goods. In such view of legal position, and when the entire matter is pending for decision in this Division, issue of such demand notice must be held to be without application of mind and uncalled for, and must be ignored at the time of final assessment of the goods to duty.

45. In the result, the Rule is disposed of in the light of above observations and directions but without any costs.

46. The concerned customs authority is directed to finally assess the goods to duty in accordance with the Customs Valuation Rules, 2000 and taking into consideration of the documents/ paper(s), if any, that may be produced on behalf of the petitioner and shall return the bank guarantee (s) if the amount, if any, that becomes due after such final assessment is paid in cash within a period of two months of receipt of this order.

Communicate at once.

End.
